title: Transporting Quantiles to Codebook: Scalable Vector Quantization without Codebook Collapse

paper.title: Transporting Quantiles to Codebook: Scalable Vector Quantization without Codebook Collapse
paper.abstract: Abstract Effective discrete representation learning with VQ-VAE serves as a fundamental component of modern autoregressive generative models. However, it is widely known to suffer from codebook collapse and inefficient code utilization. To address this issue, we propose FlowVQ, a simple yet effective alternative to standard vector quantization by formulating neural quantization as a joint modeling and clustering process. Specifically, we learn the latent space using a lightweight flow matching model alongside training, corresponding to a probability flow ODE that transports an often fixed well-behaved source distribution while preserving probability mass. Based on this, we define the codebook 𝒞 1 \mathcal{C}_{1} by transporting even-quantile partitioned prior codes 𝒞 0 \mathcal{C}_{0} from the source space through the learned flow, and obtaining the Voronoi centroids under the induced distribution, leading to a structured discretization. We evaluated on image tokenization and generation, as well as on two tasks requiring high-precision tokenization, demonstrating scalability and improved expressivity of the codebook with full utilization. Code is available at: GitHub repository .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Vector Quantized Variational AutoEncoder (VQ-VAE), proposed by Van Den Oord et al. [1] , [ 2 ] demonstrates effective discrete latent representation learning by incorporating Vector Quantization (VQ) into reconstruction. It learns a finite set of codebook vectors and tokenizes continuous data into discrete sequences by mapping to the nearest vectors, enabling large autoregressive models for continuous data generation while leveraging the design, training, and scaling principles behind large language models. By balancing fidelity, expressiveness, and computational efficiency, VQ-VAE remains an essential building block of modern generative models that are adopted across diverse domains, including state-of-the-art models for image generation and video-based world modeling. With codebook collapse and unscalable model capacity remaining unresolved, existing works have explored numerous ways to mitigate such issues. Early improvements [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] involved various training techniques such as random restart, random replacement, and k-means initialization. Williams et al. [6] and Takida et al. [7] , Takida et al. [8] proposed stochastic quantization, Zhu et al. [9] and Chang et al. [10] proposed adding an additional projector layer or bridging network after a frozen codebook. With an altered latent space, model performance can be compromised, leading to degenerate reconstruction and representation learning. Recently, Lookup-Free Quantization (LFQ) [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] methods proposed an alternative to VQ based on direct scalar quantization with fixed hypercube geometry, rounding values in each dimension to the nearest point, and showed scalable codebook capacity with improved image generation using large vocabulary sizes beyond 2 14 2^{14} . To circumvent codebook collapse, we propose that an ideal codebook should jointly model and cluster the latent space into even partitions alongside reconstruction training. The codebook vectors correspond to the Voronoi centers of these partitions, naturally allocating denser vectors to high-density regions and sparser vectors to low-density regions, regardless of the manifold geometry. This ensures full and balanced utilization, addressing expressiveness and scalability. Based on this principle, we propose a flow-based vector quantization approach without interfering with the representation learning objective. Figure 1: FlowVQ on a three-mode 2D latent distribution (K = 50): the learned flow ψ 1 γ \psi^{\gamma}_{1} transports the approximately equal-mass quantile prior codebook 𝒞 0 ∈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , I ) \mathcal{C}_{0}\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},I) , initialized using Sobol samples here and kept fixed thereafter, to the latent space. Self-correction refines each transported code using the pushed quantile samples 𝒮 1 \mathcal{S}_{1} , yielding the density-adaptive posterior codebook 𝒞 1 \mathcal{C}_{1} . A flow matching model [ 14 ] learns a continuous transport mapping samples from a prior distribution, such as a Gaussian, to an arbitrary data distribution. This transport corresponds to a Probability Flow ODE (PF-ODE) [ 15 , 16 ] , which preserves probability mass and transports prior quantiles to data quantiles. Based on this, we define the prior codebook uniformly in the well-behaved source space, and co-train the flow model with VQ-VAE. The codebook vectors are then obtained as the pushforward of the prior codebook and move toward the Voronoi centers under the estimated density. Experiments show that a lightweight flow model introduces minor overhead relative to VQ-VAE while maintaining full code utilization and improving performance. In summary, our contributions are as follows: 1. We propose FlowVQ, a novel VQ technique that converts codebook learning into a quantile transport problem, where code utilization emerges as a geometric property of the latent space, enabling balanced usage and avoiding codebook collapse. 2. We show that FlowVQ consistently achieves full codebook utilization across a range of tasks, improving reconstruction and generation quality within a unified tokenizer framework.

sections.heading: VQ-VAE & Generation in the Latent Space
sections.text: Proposed by [ 1 ] , the VQ-VAE combines vector quantization with a reconstruction objective and achieves effective neural tokenization. It enables autoregressive generation on continuous data, such as high-fidelity image generation, by predicting the sequence of tokens in the latent space using a PixelCNN [ 1 , 17 ] and, more recently transformer models. VQ-GAN [ 18 ] further couples the training with a discriminative loss, addressing the issue of blurry reconstruction from traditional VAE greatly improving generation fidelity. It has since been adopted as a standard framework. Recently, advancements on residual [ 19 ] , multi-head [ 20 ] , and multi-scale [ 21 ] tokenization were proposed and demonstrate solid improvements [ 19 , 21 , 22 ] . As a general tokenization technique, VQ-VAE based tokenizers are widely adopted in diverse generative tasks today, especially in tasks where direct generation can be prohibitively expensive such as image [ 12 , 21 , 23 ] , audio [ 3 , 24 ] , and video [ 25 , 26 ] , or in fields where structural representations are often unavailable, such as AI for protein and material generation [ 27 , 28 , 29 ] .

sections.heading: Mitigating Codebook Collapse
sections.text: To address the codebook collapse, which leads to unscalable codebook capacity, an active line of work has been proposed to mitigate it. Early work addressed it with various tricks such as random restart or random replacement [ 3 , 5 ] . Another line of work explored differentiable relaxation [ 4 , 30 , 31 ] , most notably using the Gumbel–Softmax [ 32 ] . However, these approaches generally underperform and produces lower-quality reconstruction [ 6 ] . Takida et al. [ 7 , 8 ] proposed improving the mode-dropping behavior by switching to stochastic quantization but suffer from similar unrealistic reconstructions. Zhu et al. [9] and Chang et al. [10] addressed the under-utilization issue by adding intermediate projection layer(s) between a frozen codebook and the decoder. In a parallel track, Mentzer et al. [11] , Yu et al. [12] , and Weber et al. [13] proposed LFQ, which rounds each dimension to the nearest point in a hypercube, and scales the codebook capacity with its size using direct scalar quantization. These methods demonstrate competitive or improved image generation performance, especially with large vocabulary sizes beyond 2 14 2^{14} to 2 18 2^{18} . The majority of the existing works mitigate this issue without fundamentally solving it. To our knowledge, the closest work is OptVQ [ 22 ] , which introduces global information via optimal transport between batch latents and the codebook. However, its cost matrix requires per-batch normalization for numerical stability, which distorts the transport cost inconsistently across batches. Moreover, the resulting doubly stochastic assignment is converted to a hard assignment, which does not guarantee that every code is selected, especially under stronger entropy regularization. Full utilization thus depends on the entropy weight, which trades off quantization accuracy against utilization and may be sub-optimal for a given task as observed in our experiments.

sections.heading: 3.2 Flow-based Codebook
sections.text: In this work, we propose to define the codebook in the prior space, which we call the prior codebook 𝒞 0 \mathcal{C}_{0} . The prior space can be arbitrary, as long as it supports uniform sampling. To achieve uniform sampling, we partition the prior space into K equal probability mass quantiles using its cumulative distribution function (CDF) ℱ \mathcal{F} . { 𝐂 0 i } i = 1 K \{\mathbf{C}_{0}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{K} is then obtained by applying the inverse CDF ℱ − 1 \mathcal{F}^{-1} to the centers of these quantiles: C 0 i = ℱ − 1 ( i − 0.5 K ) , i = 1 , … , K \textbf{C}_{0}^{i}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}\left(\dfrac{i-0.5}{K}\right),\quad i=1,...,K In higher dimensional latent spaces, as d increases, exact uniform quantile partitioning becomes intractable. We use Sobol sequences, a low-discrepancy quasi-random sequence designed to evenly fill multi-dimensional spaces to generate approximate uniformly distributed quantile centers. Specifically, we first generate K points in the CDF as d-dimensional unit hypercube [ 0 , 1 ] d [0,1]^{d} : { u i } i = 1 K = Sobol ​ ( K , d ) where u i ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] d \{\textbf{u}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}=\text{Sobol}(K,d)\quad\text{where}\quad\textbf{u}_{i}\in[0,1]^{d} (3) Then obtain the prior codebook for each quantile similarly C 0 i = ℱ − 1 ​ ( u i ) \textbf{C}_{0}^{i}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\textbf{u}_{i}) (4) We define the learned quantizer flow velocity field as u t γ u_{t}^{\gamma} , and the associated flow map as ψ t γ \psi_{t}^{\gamma} . Let the data distribution be x ∼ p data x\sim p_{\text{data}} . During VQ-VAE training, it is trained to match the current latent distribution over z e z_{e} with the conditional flow matching objective: ℒ FM ​ ( γ ) = 𝔼 t ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ [ 0 , 1 ] , z 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) , x ∼ p data | | u t γ ​ ( z ) − u t ​ ( z ∣ z 1 , z 0 ) | | 2 2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}}(\gamma)=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1],\ z_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}),\ x\sim p_{\text{data}}}||u_{t}^{\gamma}(z)-u_{t}(z\mid z_{1},z_{0})||_{2}^{2} (5) where d d ​ t ​ ψ t γ ​ ( z ) = u t γ ​ ( ψ t γ ​ ( z ) ) , z 1 = E θ ​ ( x ) , ψ t ​ ( z ∣ z 1 , z 0 ) = ( 1 − t ) ​ z 0 + t ​ z 1 \text{where}\quad\dfrac{d}{dt}\psi_{t}^{\gamma}(z)=u_{t}^{\gamma}(\psi_{t}^{\gamma}(z)),\quad z_{1}=E_{\theta}(x),\quad\psi_{t}(z\mid z_{1},z_{0})=(1-t)z_{0}+tz_{1} With latent distribution modeling and clustering handled by a separate flow model, the explicit codebook loss term in Eq ( 2 ) is no longer required. The flow matching objective is optimized in a decoupled manner and should introduce minimal interference to the reconstruction and quantization objectives. The overall training objective is then updated to: ℒ FlowVQ ​ ( θ , γ ) \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{FlowVQ}}(\theta,\gamma) = ℒ VQ-VAE ​ ( θ ) + ℒ FM ​ ( γ ) \displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{\text{VQ-VAE}}(\theta)\ +\ \mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}}(\gamma) (6) = ‖ D θ ​ ( STE ​ ( z q ) ) − x ‖ 2 + β ​ ‖ z e − sg ​ ( z q ) ‖ 2 + 𝔼 t , z 0 , z 1 ​ ‖ u t γ ​ ( z ) − u t ​ ( z ∣ z 1 , z 0 ) ‖ 2 \displaystyle=||D_{\theta}(\text{STE}(z_{q}))-x||^{2}\ +\ \beta||z_{e}-\text{sg}(z_{q})||^{2}\ +\ \mathbb{E}_{t,z_{0},z_{1}}||u_{t}^{\gamma}(z)-u_{t}(z\mid z_{1},z_{0})||^{2} The final codebook 𝒞 1 \mathcal{C}_{1} used in vector quantization is periodically updated. Each code vector C 1 i \textbf{C}_{1}^{i} is obtained as the pushforward of the prior codebook C 0 i \textbf{C}_{0}^{i} through the trained flow ψ t γ \psi_{t}^{\gamma} : C 1 i = ψ 1 γ ( C 0 i ) , i = 1 , … , K \textbf{C}_{1}^{i}=\psi_{1}^{\gamma}(\textbf{C}_{0}^{i}),\quad i=1,...,K (7) The codebook structure closely follows the geometry of the latent manifold and adapts to its density, naturally providing sharper resolution in denser regions and coarser in sparser regions. This is in contrast to the original VQ, which is sensitive to both initialization and training dynamics due to its reliance on both codebook and commitment losses between only matched pairs, which are a root cause of codebook collapse. Similarly, fixed-geometry approaches such as LFQ do not adapt to the latent distribution, including empty regions beyond the latent boundaries and holes within it, which limits their expressivity.

sections.heading: 3.3 Self-Correction toward Voronoi Centroids
sections.text: Up to this point, a set of approximately uniform points in the latent space is obtained through Eq ( 7 ) as the codebook 𝒞 1 \mathcal{C}_{1} , which only fulfills the first two key properties of faithful latent modeling and approximately even partitioning. To minimize the approximation error arising from the quasi-random sequence and the non-linear flow mapping, we introduce a self-correction mechanism that updates 𝒞 1 \mathcal{C}_{1} toward the Voronoi centroids as the Euclidean centers of the transported quantiles, aiming to achieve the final desired property of the codebook. This process can be viewed as transporting each quantile cell through a set of its uniformly spread samples. The trained flow serves as a proxy for the latent data distribution. Denoting N as a sampling ratio, we uniformly draw NK points { S 0 i } i = 1 N ​ K \{\textbf{S}_{0}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{NK} from the prior and push them through the flow to the latent space as dense samples 𝒮 1 \mathcal{S}_{1} similarly, simulating the incoming latent data for vector quantization as { z e ′ } \{z^{{}^{\prime}}_{e}\} . This process is analogous to k-means clustering initialized with well-chosen centers. This process is performed iteratively a few times and deterministic with minimal overhead. Optionally, we can further correct the codebook 𝒞 1 \mathcal{C}_{1} online towards the cluster centroids of real latent data { z e } \{z_{e}\} during co-training. This could reduce the remaining approximation error due to finite samples and model error. Specifically, this online correction reinstates the codebook loss of ℒ VQ-VAE \mathcal{L}_{\text{VQ-VAE}} in Eq ( 2 ) in Eq ( 6 ), which can pose a risk of re-introducing codebook collapse between two codebook updates. However, due to the quality of the flow partition and frequent codebook update, we did not observe significant collapse in our experiments and found it can further improve the model slightly over the purely self-corrected version.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: In this section, We evaluate FlowVQ on image reconstruction and generation in terms of generation quality with common metrics such as FID, IS, and codebook quality, measured by its entropy and utilization rate. We first evaluate it on CIFAR-10 [ 33 ] in Sec 4.1.1 , followed by ImageNet-1K [ 34 ] at 256 × \times 256 resolution in Sec 4.1.2 . To further examine the expressivity induced by FlowVQ and its general applicability, we evaluate FlowVQ on two high-precision tasks: crystalline material tokenization in Sec 4.2.1 , and action tokenization for robotics in Sec 4.2.2

sections.heading: 4.1.1 CIFAR-10
sections.text: As various design choices affect the final model performance, to understand the sole effect of VQ techniques, we first conduct a set of controlled experiments on CIFAR-10. All models share the same encoder and decoder architecture and training scheme (47M parameters), differing only in the quantizer, i.e., quantization and codebook update. The image is compressed to the latent space by a fixed factor f = 4 f=4 , i.e. from H × W H\times W to an H / f × W / f H/f\times W/f patch token grid. sections.heading: Result Analysis
sections.text: The results are summarized in Table 1 . We can spot the codebook collapse of the original VQ immediately when | 𝒞 | |\mathcal{C}| increases from 1024 to 10240 with a fixed latent dimension. The number of active codes decreases from 1024 × 45.6 % = 467 1024\times 45.6\%=467 to 10240 × 2.73 % = 280 10240\times 2.73\%=280 , leading to degenerate overall performance. The entropy regularization drastically improves the utilization rate of LFQ, but does not guarantee full utilization when balancing multiple objectives of minimizing quantization error and maximally filling the hypercube simultaneously. The same conflict applies to OptVQ, which was observed to learn fast in early steps, but plateaus much earlier than methods that are solely driven by the quantization objective, such as VQGAN and FlowVQ here. Nevertheless, we note that VQ-GAN serves as a strong baseline due to its flexibility, which leads to high-quality alignment between the codebook and an evolving latent space. We observe that FlowVQ achieves significant improvements in both image quality, with rFID = 1.40, reconstruction error MAE of 0.036, and codebook quality with full utilization across all settings. The performance consistently improves with increasing | 𝒞 | |\mathcal{C}| . Explicit optimizing the mutual information further improves the model slightly, though we note the performance is very close between the two. Both variants achieve the highest entropy (13.97, near the maximum l ​ o ​ g 2 ​ 16384 = 14 log_{2}{16384}=14 ), indicating the most balanced usage across codes, which validates the effectiveness of the proposed method.

sections.heading: Codebook Visualization
sections.text: We next provide visualizations of the latent space on the evaluation set and codebook alignment between FlowVQ and baselines without global information in Fig 2 . We can see the codebook collapse pattern in VQ-GAN, where a large number of codes at the bottom left remain unused despite the active codes aligning well with the latent space, while LFQ imposes a hypercube geometry, so holes in latent space inevitably lead to unused codes. FlowVQ, on the contrary, models the geometry flexibly similar to VQ-GAN and imposes no additional regularization on the latent shape, resulting in high code utilization that allows it to scale with the codebook size. For each model, the latent vectors and code vectors are randomly down-sampled to the same number, then jointly reduced to 3D using t-SNE for visualization.

sections.heading: Time Analysis
sections.text: One potential concern for the proposed method is that the pushforward operation can be time-consuming. We measure the average training time per 1000 steps (one codebook update cycle) for all models in robotics VLA model Table 6 in Appendix B . FlowVQ takes on average 618s compared to 535s for VQ-GAN, increased by 15.6% with the difference mostly due to the codebook update, which takes 82.8s on average. This time is expected to further decrease with more GPU memory. Meanwhile, as the prior vectors are pre-defined in the fixed source space, the update is fully deterministic and easily supports distributed execution with minimal communication overhead. We implement the distributed update. It takes 3s per codebook update on 32 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for | 𝒞 | = 16384 |\mathcal{C}|=16384 for large scale training such as ImageNet, thus comparable speed to the original VQ-GAN.

sections.heading: 4.2 High Precision Tokenization
sections.text: To examine the potential of an adaptive and fully utilized codebook for FlowVQ as a general tokenizer, we would like to extend the evaluation beyond the image domain. One natural task to consider is high-precision tokenization, especially where structural representation is missing and generation can greatly benefit from the discretized representation learning. Data containing geometric, motion, and spatial state information usually resides in continuous space, and small numerical differences can lead to significantly different physical states or interaction outcomes. Tokenization needs to allocate sufficient resolution to ensure that distinct physical configurations do not collapse into indistinguishable tokens. The current common practice uses k-means initialized VQ-VAE [ 27 , 28 , 29 ] . We consider two representative tasks here: crystalline material tokenization in Sec 4.2.1 and robot action tokenization in Sec 4.2.2 .

sections.heading: 4.2.1 Crystalline Material Tokenization
sections.text: We evaluate tokenization techniques for crystalline materials based on their ability to faithfully represent crystal structures using an atom-based encoder–decoder transformer. Crystals exhibit periodic atomic arrangements in 3D space and are commonly represented by a unit cell containing a set of atoms. Each atom is described by a tuple ( 𝐀 , 𝐗 , ℒ ) (\mathbf{A},\mathbf{X},\mathcal{L}) , where 𝐀 \mathbf{A} is its one-hot atom type vector, 𝐗 \mathbf{X} is its 3D fractional coordinates, and ℒ \mathcal{L} is the lattice information. These components are then concatenated into a single vector before being fed into the model. We evaluate on MP-20 [ 46 ] with | 𝒞 | = 8192 |\mathcal{C}|=8192 and d = 8. As VQ-VAE and OptVQ benefit from an aligned initialization [ 27 , 28 , 29 ] , and to isolate the effect of the quantizer, we initialize their codebooks with k-means centroids of the training-set latents from the same autoencoder at epoch W = 500, when FlowVQ quantization begins. All methods also start from the same encoder and decoder weights. For evaluation, we follow prior work [ 47 ] by comparing each reconstructed material with its ground-truth material using StructureMatcher from PyMatgen [ 48 ] and reporting the resulting match rate. We do not report codebook utilization rate for this task because MP-20 is a relatively small dataset, and the evaluation distribution does not fully cover the training distribution, which is reflected as only 7,408 of the 8,192 codes derived from the training data k-means clusters were actively used on the evaluation set. This number can further vary with the latent geometry evolving during training. We analyze the number of actively utilized codes instead. sections.heading: 4.2.2 Robotics Action Tokenization
sections.text: Robot actions in foundation models [ 49 , 50 , 51 , 52 ] have recently been represented as action chunks [ 53 , 54 ] , as fixed-length sequences of actions. Each action is represented as a vector defining the next delta movement. We evaluate on the DROID dataset [ 55 ] and compare with common action tokenizers: 1) FAST+ [ 56 ] , which applies the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) to each action dimension of a chunk, quantizes the coefficients by scaling and rounding, flattens them from low to high frequency, and compresses the resulting sequence with a pretrained Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) [ 57 , 58 ] vocabulary, 2) K-means initialized VQ-VAE. Similar to Sec 4.2.1 , we use an encoder-decoder transformer with quantization applied in the latent space. | 𝒞 | |\mathcal{C}| is set to 2048 for fair comparison with existing tokenizers, latent dimension d = 8, and more details can be found in Appendix E . sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: To summarize, we introduced FlowVQ, a vector quantization technique that reformulates codebook learning in classic VQ-VAE as a quantile-based transport process, where balanced code utilization is governed by the geometry of the latent space rather than a byproduct of auxiliary optimization objectives. By constructing the codebook via deterministic pushforwards from a uniform prior and refining them through self-correction, FlowVQ achieves stable and balanced code usage while avoiding codebook collapse. We conducted experiments across a range of tokenization and generation tasks, demonstrating consistently improved reconstruction and generation quality. We hope the proposed method will serve as a useful tool, especially in fields where features are naturally continuous or hybrid, and benefit from learned representations.

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: In addition to the slight increase in training time, FlowVQ primarily focuses on addressing codebook collapse, while another important limitation of VQ-VAE lies in the reliance on the biased STE for backpropagation through discrete quantization. Recent works have shown that this gradient mismatch can be alleviated through simple rotation tricks [ 59 ] , but more effective alternatives remain largely unexplored. Another direction worth exploring is to investigate FlowVQ together with recent architectures on flexible-length [ 60 , 61 ] or flexible-resolution [ 62 ] embedding learning, which may enable more adaptive token allocation to regions with higher semantic or structural complexity, leading to further improvements.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.34828v1 [cs.LG] 26 Oct 2026 Transporting Quantiles to Codebook: Scalable Vector Quantization without Codebook Collapse Yuwei Zeng Affiliation: National University of Singapore Zekun Shi Affiliation: National University of Singapore Affiliation: SEA AI Lab Abstract Effective discrete representation learning with VQ-VAE serves as a fundamental component of modern autoregressive generative models. However, it is widely known to suffer from codebook collapse and inefficient code utilization. To address this issue, we propose FlowVQ, a simple yet effective alternative to standard vector quantization by formulating neural quantization as a joint modeling and clustering process. Specifically, we learn the latent space using a lightweight flow matching model alongside training, corresponding to a probability flow ODE that transports an often fixed well-behaved source distribution while preserving probability mass. Based on this, we define the codebook 𝒞 1 \mathcal{C}_{1} by transporting even-quantile partitioned prior codes 𝒞 0 \mathcal{C}_{0} from the source space through the learned flow, and obtaining the Voronoi centroids under the induced distribution, leading to a structured discretization. We evaluated on image tokenization and generation, as well as on two tasks requiring high-precision tokenization, demonstrating scalability and improved expressivity of the codebook with full utilization. Code is available at: GitHub repository . 1 Introduction Vector Quantized Variational AutoEncoder (VQ-VAE), proposed by Van Den Oord et al. [1] , [ 2 ] demonstrates effective discrete latent representation learning by incorporating Vector Quantization (VQ) into reconstruction. It learns a finite set of codebook vectors and tokenizes continuous data into discrete sequences by mapping to the nearest vectors, enabling large autoregressive models for continuous data generation while leveraging the design, training, and scaling principles behind large language models. By balancing fidelity, expressiveness, and computational efficiency, VQ-VAE remains an essential building block of modern generative models that are adopted across diverse domains, including state-of-the-art models for image generation and video-based world modeling. With codebook collapse and unscalable model capacity remaining unresolved, existing works have explored numerous ways to mitigate such issues. Early improvements [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] involved various training techniques such as random restart, random replacement, and k-means initialization. Williams et al. [6] and Takida et al. [7] , Takida et al. [8] proposed stochastic quantization, Zhu et al. [9] and Chang et al. [10] proposed adding an additional projector layer or bridging network after a frozen codebook. With an altered latent space, model performance can be compromised, leading to degenerate reconstruction and representation learning. Recently, Lookup-Free Quantization (LFQ) [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] methods proposed an alternative to VQ based on direct scalar quantization with fixed hypercube geometry, rounding values in each dimension to the nearest point, and showed scalable codebook capacity with improved image generation using large vocabulary sizes beyond 2 14 2^{14} . To circumvent codebook collapse, we propose that an ideal codebook should jointly model and cluster the latent space into even partitions alongside reconstruction training. The codebook vectors correspond to the Voronoi centers of these partitions, naturally allocating denser vectors to high-density regions and sparser vectors to low-density regions, regardless of the manifold geometry. This ensures full and balanced utilization, addressing expressiveness and scalability. Based on this principle, we propose a flow-based vector quantization approach without interfering with the representation learning objective. Figure 1: FlowVQ on a three-mode 2D latent distribution (K = 50): the learned flow ψ 1 γ \psi^{\gamma}_{1} transports the approximately equal-mass quantile prior codebook 𝒞 0 ∈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , I ) \mathcal{C}_{0}\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},I) , initialized using Sobol samples here and kept fixed thereafter, to the latent space. Self-correction refines each transported code using the pushed quantile samples 𝒮 1 \mathcal{S}_{1} , yielding the density-adaptive posterior codebook 𝒞 1 \mathcal{C}_{1} . A flow matching model [ 14 ] learns a continuous transport mapping samples from a prior distribution, such as a Gaussian, to an arbitrary data distribution. This transport corresponds to a Probability Flow ODE (PF-ODE) [ 15 , 16 ] , which preserves probability mass and transports prior quantiles to data quantiles. Based on this, we define the prior codebook uniformly in the well-behaved source space, and co-train the flow model with VQ-VAE. The codebook vectors are then obtained as the pushforward of the prior codebook and move toward the Voronoi centers under the estimated density. Experiments show that a lightweight flow model introduces minor overhead relative to VQ-VAE while maintaining full code utilization and improving performance. In summary, our contributions are as follows: 1. We propose FlowVQ, a novel VQ technique that converts codebook learning into a quantile transport problem, where code utilization emerges as a geometric property of the latent space, enabling balanced usage and avoiding codebook collapse. 2. We show that FlowVQ consistently achieves full codebook utilization across a range of tasks, improving reconstruction and generation quality within a unified tokenizer framework. 2 Related Works VQ-VAE & Generation in the Latent Space Proposed by [ 1 ] , the VQ-VAE combines vector quantization with a reconstruction objective and achieves effective neural tokenization. It enables autoregressive generation on continuous data, such as high-fidelity image generation, by predicting the sequence of tokens in the latent space using a PixelCNN [ 1 , 17 ] and, more recently transformer models. VQ-GAN [ 18 ] further couples the training with a discriminative loss, addressing the issue of blurry reconstruction from traditional VAE greatly improving generation fidelity. It has since been adopted as a standard framework. Recently, advancements on residual [ 19 ] , multi-head [ 20 ] , and multi-scale [ 21 ] tokenization were proposed and demonstrate solid improvements [ 19 , 21 , 22 ] . As a general tokenization technique, VQ-VAE based tokenizers are widely adopted in diverse generative tasks today, especially in tasks where direct generation can be prohibitively expensive such as image [ 12 , 21 , 23 ] , audio [ 3 , 24 ] , and video [ 25 , 26 ] , or in fields where structural representations are often unavailable, such as AI for protein and material generation [ 27 , 28 , 29 ] . Mitigating Codebook Collapse To address the codebook collapse, which leads to unscalable codebook capacity, an active line of work has been proposed to mitigate it. Early work addressed it with various tricks such as random restart or random replacement [ 3 , 5 ] . Another line of work explored differentiable relaxation [ 4 , 30 , 31 ] , most notably using the Gumbel–Softmax [ 32 ] . However, these approaches generally underperform and produces lower-quality reconstruction [ 6 ] . Takida et al. [ 7 , 8 ] proposed improving the mode-dropping behavior by switching to stochastic quantization but suffer from similar unrealistic reconstructions. Zhu et al. [9] and Chang et al. [10] addressed the under-utilization issue by adding intermediate projection layer(s) between a frozen codebook and the decoder. In a parallel track, Mentzer et al. [11] , Yu et al. [12] , and Weber et al. [13] proposed LFQ, which rounds each dimension to the nearest point in a hypercube, and scales the codebook capacity with its size using direct scalar quantization. These methods demonstrate competitive or improved image generation performance, especially with large vocabulary sizes beyond 2 14 2^{14} to 2 18 2^{18} . The majority of the existing works mitigate this issue without fundamentally solving it. To our knowledge, the closest work is OptVQ [ 22 ] , which introduces global information via optimal transport between batch latents and the codebook. However, its cost matrix requires per-batch normalization for numerical stability, which distorts the transport cost inconsistently across batches. Moreover, the resulting doubly stochastic assignment is converted to a hard assignment, which does not guarantee that every code is selected, especially under stronger entropy regularization. Full utilization thus depends on the entropy weight, which trades off quantization accuracy against utilization and may be sub-optimal for a given task as observed in our experiments. 3 Method 3.1 Preliminary We define a codebook 𝒞 = { C i } i = 1 K \mathcal{C}=\{\textbf{C}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K} where C i ∈ ℝ d \textbf{C}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , K is the number of code vectors and d is the latent vector dimension. The prior space can be arbitrary, as long as it supports uniform sampling. To achieve uniform sampling, we partition the prior space into K equal probability mass quantiles using its cumulative distribution function (CDF) ℱ \mathcal{F} . { 𝐂 0 i } i = 1 K \{\mathbf{C}_{0}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{K} is then obtained by applying the inverse CDF ℱ − 1 \mathcal{F}^{-1} to the centers of these quantiles: C 0 i = ℱ − 1 ( i − 0.5 K ) , i = 1 , … , K \textbf{C}_{0}^{i}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}\left(\dfrac{i-0.5}{K}\right),\quad i=1,...,K In higher dimensional latent spaces, as d increases, exact uniform quantile partitioning becomes intractable. Each code vector C 1 i \textbf{C}_{1}^{i} is obtained as the pushforward of the prior codebook C 0 i \textbf{C}_{0}^{i} through the trained flow ψ t γ \psi_{t}^{\gamma} : C 1 i = ψ 1 γ ( C 0 i ) , i = 1 , … , K \textbf{C}_{1}^{i}=\psi_{1}^{\gamma}(\textbf{C}_{0}^{i}),\quad i=1,...,K (7) The codebook structure closely follows the geometry of the latent manifold and adapts to its density, naturally providing sharper resolution in denser regions and coarser in sparser regions. This is in contrast to the original VQ, which is sensitive to both initialization and training dynamics due to its reliance on both codebook and commitment losses between only matched pairs, which are a root cause of codebook collapse. Similarly, fixed-geometry approaches such as LFQ do not adapt to the latent distribution, including empty regions beyond the latent boundaries and holes within it, which limits their expressivity. 3.3 Self-Correction toward Voronoi Centroids Up to this point, a set of approximately uniform points in the latent space is obtained through Eq ( 7 ) as the codebook 𝒞 1 \mathcal{C}_{1} , which only fulfills the first two key properties of faithful latent modeling and approximately even partitioning. This process can be viewed as transporting each quantile cell through a set of its uniformly spread samples. The trained flow serves as a proxy for the latent data distribution. Denoting N as a sampling ratio, we uniformly draw NK points { S 0 i } i = 1 N ​ K \{\textbf{S}_{0}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{NK} from the prior and push them through the flow to the latent space as dense samples 𝒮 1 \mathcal{S}_{1} similarly, simulating the incoming latent data for vector quantization as { z e ′ } \{z^{{}^{\prime}}_{e}\} . One natural task to consider is high-precision tokenization, especially where structural representation is missing and generation can greatly benefit from the discretized representation learning. Data containing geometric, motion, and spatial state information usually resides in continuous space, and small numerical differences can lead to significantly different physical states or interaction outcomes. Tokenization needs to allocate sufficient resolution to ensure that distinct physical configurations do not collapse into indistinguishable tokens. The current common practice uses k-means initialized VQ-VAE [ 27 , 28 , 29 ] . We consider two representative tasks here: crystalline material tokenization in Sec 4.2.1 and robot action tokenization in Sec 4.2.2 . 4.2.1 Crystalline Material Tokenization We evaluate tokenization techniques for crystalline materials based on their ability to faithfully represent crystal structures using an atom-based encoder–decoder transformer. Crystals exhibit periodic atomic arrangements in 3D space and are commonly represented by a unit cell containing a set of atoms. Each atom is described by a tuple ( 𝐀 , 𝐗 , ℒ ) (\mathbf{A},\mathbf{X},\mathcal{L}) , where 𝐀 \mathbf{A} is its one-hot atom type vector, 𝐗 \mathbf{X} is its 3D fractional coordinates, and ℒ \mathcal{L} is the lattice information. These components are then concatenated into a single vector before being fed into the model. We evaluate on MP-20 [ 46 ] with | 𝒞 | = 8192 |\mathcal{C}|=8192 and d = 8. As VQ-VAE and OptVQ benefit from an aligned initialization [ 27 , 28 , 29 ] , and to isolate the effect of the quantizer, we initialize their codebooks with k-means centroids of the training-set latents from the same autoencoder at epoch W = 500, when FlowVQ quantization begins. All methods also start from the same encoder and decoder weights. For evaluation, we follow prior work [ 47 ] by comparing each reconstructed material with its ground-truth material using StructureMatcher from PyMatgen [ 48 ] and reporting the resulting match rate. We do not report codebook utilization rate for this task because MP-20 is a relatively small dataset, and the evaluation distribution does not fully cover the training distribution, which is reflected as only 7,408 of the 8,192 codes derived from the training data k-means clusters were actively used on the evaluation set. This number can further vary with the latent geometry evolving during training. We analyze the number of actively utilized codes instead. With details in Sec 3.3 , sc refers to self-correction mechanism, and oc refers to the optional online-correction mechanism. 5 Conclusion To summarize, we introduced FlowVQ, a vector quantization technique that reformulates codebook learning in classic VQ-VAE as a quantile-based transport process, where balanced code utilization is governed by the geometry of the latent space rather than a byproduct of auxiliary optimization objectives. By constructing the codebook via deterministic pushforwards from a uniform prior and refining them through self-correction, FlowVQ achieves stable and balanced code usage while avoiding codebook collapse. We conducted experiments across a range of tokenization and generation tasks, demonstrating consistently improved reconstruction and generation quality. We hope the proposed method will serve as a useful tool, especially in fields where features are naturally continuous or hybrid, and benefit from learned representations. Limitations and Future Work In addition to the slight increase in training time, FlowVQ primarily focuses on addressing codebook collapse, while another important limitation of VQ-VAE lies in the reliance on the biased STE for backpropagation through discrete quantization. Recent works have shown that this gradient mismatch can be alleviated through simple rotation tricks [ 59 ] , but more effective alternatives remain largely unexplored. Another direction worth exploring is to investigate FlowVQ together with recent architectures on flexible-length [ 60 , 61 ] or flexible-resolution [ 62 ] embedding learning, which may enable more adaptive token allocation to regions with higher semantic or structural complexity, leading to further improvements.
